terms: Appendicular skeleton
Bones of arms, legs, shoulder and pelvic girdles; enables movement.
Axial skeleton
Skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum; protects vital organs.
Joint
Where two or more bones meet; classified by type and movement.
Ligament
Tough connective tissue joining bone to bone, stabilising joints.
Skeleton
Internal framework of 206 bones providing support, movement, protection and blood-cell production.
Synovial joint
Freely movable joint with synovial fluid; e.g., hinge (elbow), ball-and-socket (hip).
Agility
Ability to change direction quickly while maintaining control.
Cardiovascular endurance
Heart and lungs supply O2 to working muscles over prolonged exercise.
Flexibility
Range of motion at a joint, influenced by muscles, tendons and joint structure.
Muscular endurance
Ability of muscles to sustain repeated contractions over time.
Muscular strength
Maximum force a muscle or group can exert in one contraction.
Speed
Rate at which a body can move from one point to another; depends on muscle fibres and technique.
Closed skill
A self-paced skill performed in a stable, predictable environment not affected by opponents, such as a free throw or a serve.
Distributed practice
Practice broken up with rest or alternative activities, best suited to beginners, complex skills and tasks that are tiring or dangerous.
Extrinsic feedback
Information about performance from an outside source such as a coach, teammate or video, important for beginners who cannot yet judge their own technique.
Feedback
Information a performer receives about a performance; it can be intrinsic (felt internally) or extrinsic (from others), and positive or negative.
Massed practice
Continuous practice without rest intervals, best suited to simple, discrete, closed skills and to fit, experienced performers.
Open skill
A skill performed in an unpredictable environment constantly affected by surroundings, such as a pass in football, requiring the performer to adapt.
Part practice
Breaking a complex skill into sections and practising each separately before linking them, useful for difficult or dangerous skills.
SMART goals
Targets that are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic and Time-bound, used to structure improvement and maintain motivation in practical performance.
Skill
A learned action aimed at achieving a result with maximum certainty and efficiency, usually with minimum effort, developed through practice.
Whole practice
Practising a skill in its complete form without breaking it down, suitable for simple skills that cannot easily be split into parts.
Discrimination
Unfair treatment based on race, gender, religion, disability or sexuality.
Equality
Equal access and opportunity for all participants regardless of personal characteristics.
Etiquette
Unwritten rules of conduct in a sport (e.g., shaking hands at the net).
Hooliganism
Violent or disorderly behaviour by sports fans, especially around football.
Sportsmanship
Fair play, respect for opponents, officials and the spirit of the game.
Stereotype
Oversimplified belief about a group, e.g., 'girls can't play football'.
Ancient Olympic Games
Held at Olympia, Greece from 776 BCE; centred on a religious festival to Zeus.
Football Association
Founded 1863 in London; first national governing body of football.
Industrial Revolution and sport
Created leisure time, mass spectators, factory teams; transport allowed national leagues.
Modern Olympics
Revived by Pierre de Coubertin in Athens, 1896.
Professionalism in cricket / football
Late 19th-century shift away from amateurism; debates continue today.
Public school athleticism
Victorian English public schools codified games like rugby, football, cricket.
Continuous data
Quantitative data that can take any value within a range, such as time, mass or temperature, and is usually measured rather than counted.
Discrete data
Quantitative data that can only take certain separate values, usually whole numbers, such as the number of goals scored in a match.
Primary data
Information collected first-hand by the performer or researcher, for example recording your own resting heart rate during a fitness test.
Qualitative data
Descriptive, non-numerical data about quality or opinion, such as a coach's judgement of technique, which is subjective and harder to compare.
Quantitative data
Numerical data that can be measured or counted, such as heart rate in beats per minute or distance in metres, allowing objective comparison.
Secondary data
Information collected by someone else and then used by the performer, such as published normative fitness tables or official match statistics.
ATP
Adenosine triphosphate: universal energy molecule for muscle contraction; reserves last ~2 seconds.
ATP-PC system
Phosphocreatine breakdown rephosphorylates ADP to ATP; provides energy for ~10 seconds, all-out efforts.
Aerobic system
With O2: glucose + O2 -> CO2 + H2O + energy; sustainable for hours, low intensity.
Anaerobic glycolysis
Without O2: glucose -> 2 lactate + energy; lasts ~10-180 s, high intensity.
Lactate
Anaerobic by-product associated with muscle fatigue (former 'lactic acid').
Oxygen debt (EPOC)
Excess Post-exercise Oxygen Consumption: O2 needed after exercise to restore systems.
Balanced diet
Eating the right amount of energy and the correct proportions of carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water for good health.
Cardiovascular fitness
The ability of the heart, lungs and blood vessels to deliver oxygen to working muscles during sustained exercise; also called aerobic endurance.
Fitness
The ability to meet the demands of the environment and everyday tasks, often measured through components such as strength, stamina and flexibility.
Health
A state of complete physical, mental and social wellbeing, not merely the absence of disease or infirmity, as defined by the World Health Organisation.
Obesity
A condition of carrying excess body fat to the point that health is harmed, commonly identified by a body mass index (BMI) above 30.
Sedentary lifestyle
A way of living involving little or no physical activity, which raises the risk of obesity, heart disease and type 2 diabetes.
FITT principle
A framework for planning training that adjusts Frequency, Intensity, Time and Type to ensure improvement and avoid plateaus.
Personal exercise programme (PEP)
A structured training plan built around an individual's goals, current fitness and chosen activity, applying the principles of training over a set period.
Progressive overload
Gradually increasing the demands placed on the body during training so that fitness keeps improving without causing injury.
Recovery
The rest the body needs between training sessions to adapt and repair, preventing overtraining and reducing the risk of injury.
Reversibility
The principle that fitness gains are lost when training stops or intensity drops, so improvements decline if a programme is not maintained.
Specificity
The principle that training should match the demands of the chosen activity, working the relevant muscles, energy systems and skills.

Bones of arms, legs, shoulder and pelvic girdles; enables movement.
Axial skeleton
Skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum; protects vital organs.
Joint
Where two or more bones meet; classified by type and movement.
Ligament
Tough connective tissue joining bone to bone, stabilising joints.
Skeleton
Internal framework of 206 bones providing support, movement, protection and blood-cell production.
Synovial joint
Freely movable joint with synovial fluid; e.g., hinge (elbow), ball-and-socket (hip).
